figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: AutoGen enables diverse LLM-based applications using multi-agent conversations. (Left) AutoGen agents are conversable, customizable, and can be based on LLMs, tools, humans, or even a combination of them. (Top-middle) Agents can converse to solve tasks. (Right) They can form a chat, potentially with humans in the loop. (Bottom-middle) The framework supports flexible conversation patterns.
figures.headline: AutoGen agents backed by LLMs, tools or humans converse to solve tasks, with humans optionally in the loop.
citing_sentences: While there is contemporaneous exploration of multi-agent approaches, we present AutoGen, a generalized multi-agent conversation framework (Figure 1), based on the following new concepts.
In the example on the right-hand side of Figure 1, an LLM-backed assistant agent and a tool- and human-backed user proxy agent are deployed together to tackle a task.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Illustration of how to use AutoGen to program a multi-agent conversation. The top sub-figure illustrates the built-in agents provided by AutoGen, which have unified conversation interfaces and can be customized. The middle sub-figure shows an example of using AutoGen to develop a two-agent system with a custom reply function. The bottom sub-figure illustrates the resulting automated agent chat from the two-agent system during program execution.
figures.headline: A two-agent system with a custom reply function runs its conversation automatically once started, as the code and dialog show.
citing_sentences: The yellow-shaded area of Figure 2 provides a sketch of the built-in agents in AutoGen.
Figure 2 provides a simple illustration.

For example, with the developer code in the blue-shaded area (marked “Developer Code”) of Figure 2, one can readily trigger the conversation among the agents, and the conversation would proceed automatically, as shown in the dialog box in the grey shaded area (marked “Program Execution”) of Figure 2.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Six examples of diverse applications built using AutoGen. Their conversation patterns show AutoGen’s flexibility and power.
figures.headline: Six applications built with AutoGen show conversation patterns ranging from two-agent chats to group chats and chess.
citing_sentences: We provide implemented working systems to showcase all these different patterns, with some of them visualized in Figure 3.
We demonstrate six applications using AutoGen (see Figure 3) to illustrate its potential in simplifying the development of high-performance multi-agent applications.
The second sub-figure of Figure 3 shows the AutoGen-based implementation.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Performance on four applications A1-A4. (a) shows that AutoGen agents can be used out of the box to achieve the most competitive performance on math problem solving tasks; (b) shows that AutoGen can be used to realize effective retrieval augmentation and realize a novel interactive retrieval feature to boost performance on Q&A tasks; (c) shows that AutoGen can be used to introduce a three-agent system with a grounding agent to improve performance on ALFWorld; (d) shows that a multi-agent design is helpful in boosting performance in coding tasks that need safeguards.
figures.headline: AutoGen-based systems perform competitively on math, retrieval, decision making and coding safeguard tasks.
citing_sentences: We evaluate our system and several alternative approaches, including open-source methods such as Multi-Agent Debate Liang et al. (2023), LangChain ReAct LangChain (2023), vanilla GPT-4, and commercial products ChatGPT + Code Interpreter, and ChatGPT + Plugin (Wolfram Alpha), on the MATH Hendrycks et al. (2021) dataset and summarize the results in Figure 4(a).
(Scenario 1) We first perform an evaluation regarding natural question answering on the Natural Questions dataset Kwiatkowski et al. (2019) and report results in Figure 4(b).

We conduct an ablation study in which we prompt the assistant agent to say “I don’t know” instead of “UPDATE CONTEXT.” in cases where relevant information is not found, and report results in Figure 4(b).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Default system message for the built-in assistant agent in AutoGen (v0.1.1). This is an example of conversation programming via natural language. It contains instructions of different types, including role play, control flow, output confine, facilitate automation, and grounding.
figures.headline: The default assistant system message combines role play, control flow, output confinement, automation and grounding instructions.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 shows the default system message for the built-in assistant agent in AutoGen (v0.1.1), where we introduce several new prompting techniques and highlight them accordingly.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Examples of three settings utilized to solve math problems using AutoGen: (Gray) Enables a workflow where a student collaborates with an assistant agent to solve problems, either autonomously or in a human-in-the-loop mode. (Gray + Orange) Facilitates a more sophisticated workflow wherein the assistant, on the fly, can engage another user termed “expert”, who is in the loop with their own assistant agent, to aid in problem-solving if its own solutions are not satisfactory.
figures.headline: Math workflows start as a student and assistant pair, then add an expert agent when the assistant's solutions are unsatisfactory.
citing_sentences: A detailed visualization is shown in Figure 6.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Overview of Retrieval-augmented Chat which involves two agents, including a Retrieval-augmented User Proxy and a Retrieval-augmented Assistant. Given a set of documents, the Retrieval-augmented User Proxy first automatically processes documents—splits, chunks, and stores them in a vector database. Then for a given user input, it retrieves relevant chunks as context and sends it to the Retrieval-augmented Assistant, which uses LLM to generate code or text to answer questions. Agents converse until they find a satisfactory answer.
figures.headline: Retrieval-augmented Chat has a user proxy that stores documents in a vector database, and an assistant that answers from retrieved chunks.
citing_sentences: The workflow of Retrieval-Augmented Chat is illustrated in Figure 7.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Retrieval-augmented Chat without (W/O) and with (W/) interactive retrieval.
figures.headline: An example shows interactive retrieval with and without the feature on a Natural Questions case.
citing_sentences: An example (Figure 8) from the NQ dataset showcases the advantages of the interactive retrieval feature: “who carried the usa flag in opening ceremony”.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: We use AutoGen to solve tasks in the ALFWorld benchmark, which contains household tasks described in natural language. We propose two designs: a two-agent design where the assistant agent suggests the next step, and the Executor executes actions and provides feedback. The three-agent design adds a grounding agent that supplies commonsense facts to the executor when needed.
figures.headline: The three-agent ALFWorld design adds a grounding agent that supplies commonsense facts to the executor when needed.
citing_sentences: We first propose a straightforward two-agent system with AutoGen, illustrated on the left-hand side of Figure 9, to tackle tasks from this benchmark.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Comparison of results from two designs: (a) Two-agent design which consists of an assistant and an executor, (b) Three-agent design which adds a grounding agent that serves as a knowledge source. For simplicity, we omit the in-context examples and part of the exploration trajectory, and only show parts contributing to the failure/success of the attempt.
figures.headline: Trajectories show a grounding agent helps prevent the assistant from confusing finding an object with taking it.
citing_sentences: For an example trajectory comparing the systems see Appendix D, Figure 10.
Figure 10 exemplifies how a three-agent design eliminates one root cause for failure cases.
Without a grounding agent, the assistant frequently conflates finding an object with taking it, as illustrated in Figure 10a).

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Our re-implementation of OptiGuide with AutoGen streamlining agents’ interactions. The Commander receives user questions (e.g., What if we prohibit shipping from supplier 1 to roastery 2?) and coordinates with the Writer and Safeguard. The Writer crafts the code and interpretation, the Safeguard ensures safety (e.g., not leaking information, no malicious code), and the Commander executes the code. If issues arise, the process can repeat until resolved. Shaded circles represent steps that may be repeated multiple times.
figures.headline: The OptiGuide re-implementation has a Commander coordinate a Writer and Safeguard, repeating steps until questions are resolved.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: A5: Dynamic Group Chat: Overview of how AutoGen enables dynamic group chats to solve tasks. The Manager agent, which is an instance of the GroupChatManager class, performs the following three steps–select a single speaker (in this case Bob), ask the speaker to respond, and broadcast the selected speaker’s message to all other agents
figures.headline: A group chat manager selects one speaker, collects its response and broadcasts it to all other agents.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Comparison of two-agent chat (a) and group chat (b) on a given task. The group chat resolves the task successfully with a smoother conversation, while the two-agent chat fails on the same task and ends with a repeated conversation.
figures.headline: Group chat resolves a task that two-agent chat fails, which ends in a repeated conversation.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: A6: Conversational Chess: Our conversational chess application can support various scenarios, as each player can be an LLM-empowered AI, a human, or a hybrid of the two. Here, the board agent maintains the rules of the game and supports the players with information about the board. Players and the board agent all use natural language for communication.
figures.headline: Conversational Chess supports AI, human and hybrid players, with a board agent that keeps the rules and board state.
citing_sentences: Figure 14 illustrates the scenarios supported by Conversational Chess: AI/human vs. AI/human, and demonstrates how players and the board agent interact.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Example conversations during a game involving two AI player agents and a board agent.
figures.headline: Example game between two AI players and a board agent shows conversation the text calls natural and entertaining.
citing_sentences: An illustrative example of these entertaining game dynamics can be found in Figure 15, Appendix D. (2) Grounding, which is a crucial aspect to maintain game integrity.

This setup fosters social interaction and allows players to express their moves creatively, employing jokes, meme references, and character-playing, thereby making chess games more entertaining for both players and observers (Figure 15 provides an example of conversational chess).
As shown in Figure 15, the conversation between AI players can be natural and entertaining.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: Comparison of two designs–(a) without a board agent, and (b) with a board agent–in Conversational Chess.
figures.headline: Without a board agent, illegitimate moves disrupt Conversational Chess games, while the version with one avoids this.
citing_sentences: To illustrate the effect facilitated by this board agent, we provide a demonstration of conversational chess without a board agent in Figure 16.

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: We use AutoGen to build MiniWobChat, which solves tasks in the MiniWob++ benchmark. MiniWobChat consists of two agents: an assistant agent and an executor agent. The assistant agent suggests actions to manipulate the browser while the executor executes the suggested actions and returns rewards/feedback. The assistant agent records the feedback and continues until the feedback indicates task success or failure.
figures.headline: MiniWobChat pairs an assistant agent suggesting browser actions with an executor returning rewards and feedback.
citing_sentences: We designed a straightforward two-agent system named MiniWobChat using AutoGen, as shown in Figure 17.

figures.label: Figure 18
figures.caption: Comparisons between RCI (state-of-the-art prior work) and MiniWobChat on the MiniWob++ benchmark are elucidated herein. We utilize all available tasks in the official RCI code, each with varying degrees of difficulty, to conduct comprehensive comparisons. For each task, the success rate across ten different instances is reported. The results reveal that MiniWobChat attains a performance comparable to that of RCI. When a success rate tolerance of 0.1 is considered for each task, both methods outperform each other on an equal number of tasks.
figures.headline: MiniWobChat reaches performance comparable to RCI across MiniWob++ tasks, with success rates over ten instances per task.
citing_sentences: Figure 18 illustrates that MiniWobChat achieves competitive performance in this evaluation.
It is worth noting that in most tasks, the difference between the two methods is mirrored as shown in Figure 18.

abstract: AutoGen is an open-source framework that allows developers to build LLM applications via multiple agents that can converse with each other to accomplish tasks. AutoGen agents are customizable, conversable, and can operate in various modes that employ combinations of LLMs, human inputs, and tools. Using AutoGen, developers can also flexibly define agent interaction behaviors. Both natural language and computer code can be used to program flexible conversation patterns for different applications. AutoGen serves as a generic framework for building diverse applications of various complexities and LLM capacities. Empirical studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework in many example applications, with domains ranging from mathematics, coding, question answering, operations research, online decision-making, entertainment, etc.

sections.body: The introduction argues that multi-agent conversation can support LLM applications across many domains and complexities. It gives three reasons: chat-optimized LLMs incorporate feedback, a single LLM covers a broad range of capabilities, and LLMs solve complex tasks when they are broken into subtasks. The paper asks how to design capable, customizable agents and a unified interface for many conversation patterns. Its two new concepts are customizable and conversable agents, which can use LLMs, humans and tools, and conversation programming, which defines agent interactions in natural language or code. The section says the evaluation in Section 3 and Appendix D shows AutoGen can achieve outstanding performance on many tasks while reducing development effort.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Multi-agent conversation is proposed as the basis for building LLM applications, implemented in the AutoGen framework.

sections.body: Section 2 defines a conversable agent as an entity that sends and receives messages and can use LLMs, humans or tools. AutoGen provides ConversableAgent, with AssistantAgent and UserProxyAgent as pre-configured subclasses. Conversation programming specifies computation, meaning agent actions, and control flow, meaning conversation-driven decisions. Agents share unified send, receive and `generate_reply` interfaces. An auto-reply mechanism proceeds without a separate control plane once reply functions are registered. Control can be written in natural language in system messages or in Python, for example the maximum number of auto replies. Dynamic patterns use custom reply functions, LLM-driven function calls, or the GroupChatManager class.
sections.heading: The AutoGen Framework
sections.headline: AutoGen rests on conversable agents and conversation programming, where agents exchange messages and control flow emerges from those conversations.

sections.body: Six applications, labeled A1 to A6, illustrate AutoGen. For math (A1), two built-in agents were tested on 120 randomly selected level-5 problems and on the full test set, and the text reports better out-of-the-box performance than the alternatives. Retrieval-augmented Chat (A2) adds an interactive retrieval feature. For ALFWorld decision making (A3), a grounding agent gives a 15% performance gain on average over 134 unseen tasks. For coding (A4), the core OptiGuide workflow code was reduced from over 430 lines to 100 lines, and a multi-agent design raised the F-1 score for identifying unsafe code by 8% with GPT-4 and 35% with GPT-3.5-turbo. A5 is dynamic group chat and A6 is Conversational Chess.
sections.heading: Applications of AutoGen
sections.headline: Six example applications test AutoGen across math, retrieval, decision making, coding, group chat and chess.

sections.body: The discussion summarizes AutoGen as a library built on conversable agents, a unified conversation interface and auto-reply mechanisms. It reports, citing Section 3, improved performance, reduced development code and less manual burden for existing applications. It states the work is in early experimental stages. Future directions include integrating existing agent implementations, balancing automation and human control, and studying agent topology and conversation patterns. It notes that more agents and other degrees of freedom may introduce new safety challenges that need further study and careful consideration.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The discussion frames AutoGen as a general framework and states that its experiments are early, with safety questions left open.

sections.body: The ethics statement lists five considerations. Privacy and data protection concern user data and conversations when humans take part in agent chats. Bias and fairness concern biases in LLM training data appearing in agent conversations. Accountability and transparency call for mechanisms that let users trace agent decision making. Trust and reliance concern how automation affects user experience and dependence on AI, and call for clear communication of capabilities and limits. Unintended consequences concern agents changing external environments through code execution or function calls, such as installing packages, which the statement says could be risky.
sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.headline: The ethics statement names privacy, bias, accountability, trust and unintended consequences as risks to address.

sections.body: The appendix contains a related work section that groups single-agent and multi-agent systems and compares AutoGen with multi-agent systems in a table covering infrastructure, conversation pattern, execution capability and human involvement. It then gives an expanded discussion of why the applications benefit from ease of use, modularity, programmability, human involvement and collaborative or adversarial interactions. Usage guidelines recommend starting with built-in agents and simple topologies. The future work section raises questions on optimal multi-agent workflows and highly capable agents. Supporting figures show the system messages, workflows and results of the applications.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers related work with a comparison table, expanded discussion, usage guidelines, future work, and supporting figures.
